I could not execute 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs' myself (no Bash in this turn's tool grant — the same structural gap noted in prior turns' findings on lp-dfad42 and lp-138b76), so I cannot directly confirm the gate passes. Confidence is high because this is a mechanical extension of an already-passing loop over SOLID_NAMES using functions (constellation, verify) already exercised for all five solids elsewhere in the same file, and the ticket itself states the fix is exact by construction for any aniso — but this is inference, not execution, and I'm flagging it honestly rather than claiming a verified pass.

beads.title: Apply the yaw-exactness check to a solid whose normals are NOT axis-aligned
beads.body:
Bounded paths: plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs only, no changes to plant/solids.mjs. The 'determinism and orientation' block (~lines 75-88) checks that a yawed constellation stays exact (verify(r1).ok) using only 'cube'. plant/solids.mjs's own header comment names the exact trap this repeats: cube's normals are axis-aligned, the one case an anisotropic metric cannot rotate wrong — 'the worst possible outcome... the first solid anyone tries is the cube, it looks perfect, and the bug waits in the second one.' That trap applies just as much to testing yaw() as it did to the original constellation bug: a yaw() sign error or axis error could still pass this block today because cube's axis-aligned faces don't exercise it fully in the same way icosahedron or dodecahedron would. Add the same yaw-then-verify pair (rotate=0 vs rotate=Math.PI/5 or similar) for icosahedron in addition to cube, asserting both 'a yaw actually moves the seeds' and 'a yawed solid is still exact' and 'yaw preserves the inradius' for it, matching the existing cube assertions' style. Ties directly to the FINDING that a verifier grading against the wrong (unrotated) reference failed correct geometry by exactly the yaw angle — this proposal is choosing a harder solid so that class of bug can't hide behind cube's symmetry a second time. Independent of the other two proposals (different block, no shared code). Reversible: pure test-file addition.

[turn 4 — done] Added the same yaw-then-verify pair that already covers cube, but for icosahedron, in the 'determinism and orientation' block of plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs — no other file touched. icosahedron's normals are not axis-aligned (unlike cube's), so this exercises yaw() against foam's anisotropic metric in a way the cube-only block could not: a yaw() sign or axis error could in principle still pass the cube pair while failing here. The three new assertions mirror the existing cube ones exactly: rotate=0 vs rotate=Math.PI/5 seeds differ, the yawed constellation is still verify().ok, and the inradius is preserved. This turn has no Bash tool, so 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs' (the ticket's own GATE) could not be executed in-turn — confidence rests on the new code being structurally identical to the pre-existing, already-passing cube block, using the same constellation()/verify() functions already exercised elsewhere in this file for icosahedron (just without rotate). This is unverified-in-turn, not unverified in principle.

beads.title: class-A's gate certifies no regression, not the new behaviour — the agent writes the assertions it is graded by
beads.body:
Observed at the moment of promoting lp-6b641c/lp-687d8d/lp-138b76, the loop's first self-made queue.

All three name the SAME gate: 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs'. It exists today and it passes today, which is what makes them class-A. But their bounded paths include plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs itself, so the agent adds the assertions and then is graded by them. The gate proves NOTHING NEW BROKE; it does not prove the new exports are correct, because nothing tested them until the same turn wrote both sides.

This is not a reason to refuse them — a gate that catches regression is worth running, and refusing every ticket whose test does not pre-exist means only work with a pre-written test is ever schedulable, which is a much smaller loop than the one being built. It IS the reason to keep the judge's adversarial signal, and it is the sharpest argument for a REVIEW seat that reads the diff rather than trusting the exit code.

Ranked by exposure: lp-6b641c is worst (new executable exports, self-authored tests). lp-687d8d and lp-138b76 only widen coverage of code that already exists and is already verified against a closed-form answer, so their self-certification is much weaker tea.

Watch for: a turn that makes the gate pass by weakening an assertion rather than by doing the work. That is the specific cheat this shape permits and the one the verdict should look for.

[turn ? — done] Operator dry-run of the ask channel, applied through the real validator rather than hand-written into the ledger — the same code path an agent's outbox takes.

beads.title: pairGap uses conA.aniso, not an aniso argument of its own
beads.body: The ticket's signature is pairGap(conA, conB) -- two args, no aniso. Two constellations being checked against each other are expected to live in the same pocket and therefore share one metric, so I read it off conA rather than requiring the caller to pass it again or silently defaulting to something that could disagree with either constellation's own aniso. Rejected: a third optional aniso parameter (drifts from the ticket's stated signature for no real benefit) and asserting conA.aniso === conB.aniso (extra failure mode for a case that in practice can't arise -- both constellations come from the same constellation() call site in the same pocket). This reverses easily if a caller ever legitimately mixes metrics: add the parameter back with conA.aniso as its default.

beads.title: cube's minimum self-seed-gap is EXACTLY 2*r, no approximation -- because aniso only touches y and cube neighbours never mix y with x or z
beads.body: constellation('cube', {r}) places neighbours at exactly (+-2r,0,0),(0,+-2r,0),(0,0,+-2r) -- the t=2r/q algebra collapses to that because q=1 for an axis-aligned unit normal. The centre-to-x-or-z-neighbour seedGap is then hypot(2r,0,0)=2r with zero anisotropic scaling involved (dy=0), and every other pair (neighbour-neighbour, or centre to a y-axis neighbour) is provably larger since sqrt(aniso)>1 only inflates gaps that involve a y-difference. So for the cube specifically, 'is it self-compatible at minSeedGap m' reduces to the exact closed form r >= m/2 -- no floating-point approximation risk, unlike every other solid in SOLIDS. Worth knowing if a future ticket wants a cheap, exact clearance check for the one solid the anisotropic trap doesn't touch.

beads.title: Add a closed-form fast path or documented formula for cube self-compatibility (r >= minSeedGap/2) alongside the general selfCompatible
beads.body: Filed as a finding on this same turn: cube's own-seed minimum gap is exactly 2*r for any aniso, because its normals are axis-aligned and aniso only scales the y-axis. That's a decidable predicate in closed form, unlike the other four solids. Not urgent -- selfCompatible(con) already gets the right answer for cube today by brute force over 7 seeds, this would only matter if a hot path needed to test many candidate cube radii without allocating a constellation each time.

beads.title: Grant Bash (or a downstream verification turn) to class-A tickets whose GATE is a shell command, or make the gate's in-turn-unverified status explicit in the bead
beads.body: Second turn in a row (after lp-dfad42) where the ticket's own acceptance test (node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs) could not be run by the turn responsible for satisfying it, because the tool grant is Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only. This isn't a complaint about this specific ticket -- the port and this export both had enough closed-form structure to hand-verify with real confidence -- but a ticket whose new code is more novel or less analytically tractable than this one would have no way to self-check at all. Either the executing turn for a node-gated class-A bead should get Bash, or the bead should say up front that gate verification happens downstream (CI or the judge) so the turn doesn't have to pretend confidence it can't back up.

beads.title: This turn's own gate is unverifiable in-turn — same shape as lp-dfad42
beads.body: lp-138b76's GATE is 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs' but this turn's tool grant was Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash. The added assertions are a mechanical copy of the existing, already-passing cube yaw block with 'cube'->'icosahedron' and r 1.5->1.2, calling the same constellation()/verify() functions already proven correct for icosahedron elsewhere in the same file (just without rotate) — so confidence is high, but it is inference from adjacent evidence, not execution. Confirms the earlier finding that class-A tickets whose gate is a shell command need either a Bash-equipped turn or an explicit downstream (CI/judge) verification step, not an in-turn assumption that the gate ran.

beads.title: Turn 3's self-authored tests killed 2 of 3 mutants — the survivor is the one behaviour it strengthened
beads.body:
Mutation-tested turn 3's output (lp-6b641c) rather than trusting its green gate, because lp-20c414 flagged that the agent writes the assertions it is graded by.

  seedGap drops the sqrt(aniso) scaling  -> KILLED
  pairGap returns max instead of min     -> KILLED
  selfCompatible skips the centre seed   -> SURVIVED

The survivor matters more than the two kills. selfCompatible's docstring claims it checks 'its centre AND every neighbour', and that IS a deliberate strengthening over the inline loop it replaced, which only checked neighbour-vs-neighbour. The agent widened the contract, documented the widening, and then tested only the part that was already true. Every solid it asserts on has its centre comfortably clear of its own neighbours at r=1.0, so removing the centre from the loop changes no verdict in the suite.

The verdict on the turn is still GOOD: correct against foamworld.js:721-722 (which compares the squared form to 2.25, so the un-squared < 1.5 is exactly equivalent), foam/ untouched, every new positive paired with a CONTROL negative, and the replaced assertions strictly stronger than the ones removed.

The generalisable lesson, which is worth more than the fix: a self-certifying turn tests what it BUILT and under-tests what it CLAIMED. The gap is not in the code, it is between the docstring and the assertions. A review seat should diff those two against each other.

beads.title: Assert selfCompatible's centre-inclusion — the one claim turn 3 documented but did not test
beads.body:
Bounded paths: plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs ONLY. Do not change plant/solids.mjs — the implementation is correct; the suite just cannot tell.

Mutation testing (see lp-c46a0c) showed that changing selfCompatible's loop from con.seeds to con.neighbours — i.e. silently dropping the centre seed it promises to check — leaves every assertion in the suite passing. Its docstring says 'its centre AND every neighbour'; nothing proves the first half.

Add a case where the CENTRE is the violating seed while all neighbour-vs-neighbour gaps stay legal, so selfCompatible must return false for a reason only centre-inclusion can see. A flattened constellation is the natural shape: keep r large enough that the neighbours stay mutually clear, and pick a solid/aniso where at least one neighbour falls within 1.5 of the centre under the anisotropic metric. Assert false, and pair it with a CONTROL that is identical except comfortably clear, asserting true — the file's house style, and the thing that proves the new case fails for the intended reason rather than by accident.

Verify your case actually has teeth before reporting done: it must FAIL if selfCompatible iterates con.neighbours instead of con.seeds. If you cannot construct such a case for any solid, that is a real finding about the geometry — file it as one and say why, rather than forcing a weaker assertion.

[turn 6 — done] Added a centre-inclusion test to plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs, the only file the ticket permits touching. Used a cube constellation at r=0.7, aniso=2.2: cube's centre-to-(x or z)-neighbour gap is exactly 2r (no anisotropic scaling, since that pair never differs in y), while its smallest neighbour-vs-neighbour gap is 2r*sqrt(2) (between two neighbours on perpendicular non-y axes, all other pairs larger). Those two floors diverge with r, giving a window (0.5303... <= r < 0.75) where the centre fails the 1.5 seed-gap threshold while every neighbour-vs-neighbour pair still clears it. Hand-verified every distance from the closed-form seedGap/constellation algebra (not executed, no Bash available): centre gap = 1.4 < 1.5; minimum neighbour-neighbour gap = 2*0.7*sqrt(2) ~= 1.9799 >= 1.5, computed and cross-checked across all 15 neighbour pairs. Asserted selfCompatible(centreOnly, 1.5) is false, paired with a CONTROL at r=0.8 (centre gap becomes 1.6 >= 1.5) asserting true, plus two setup assertions confirming the fixture's own preconditions (centre gap below threshold, all neighbour gaps above) so the case's teeth are visible in the test output itself, not just inferred. This case fails under the documented mutant (selfCompatible iterating con.neighbours instead of con.seeds) because that mutant would skip the centre entirely and see only the legal neighbour-neighbour gaps, returning true where the correct answer is false. Did not modify plant/solids.mjs — the implementation was already correct per lp-c46a0c's mutation testing; only the suite was missing this case. Test was not executed in this turn (Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash) — confidence is high from hand-derived closed-form algebra plus the existing recorded finding that cube's non-y centre-neighbour gap is exactly 2r and is that constellation's global minimum, but this should be confirmed by running the gate.

beads.title: The reactor was the one writer that pushed without rebasing — a concurrent commit stops the whole chain
beads.body:
Turn 4's verdict woke the tick, the tick correctly decided "dispatch" for turn 5, and then died in its push loop because an operator commit had landed while it was deciding. The chain stopped with a red run on a CORRECT decision.

loop-work and loop-judge both retry as "git pull --rebase && git push". loop-tick retried a bare "git push" four times. Nothing between those attempts can turn a non-fast-forward into a fast-forward, so the retry loop was four guaranteed failures with exponential backoff between them — a backoff that could only ever make the loss slower.

Three things this says beyond the one-line fix:

1. THE RETRY WAS DECORATIVE. It looked like resilience and had none. Backoff without a merge step is a spin. Any retry loop in this repo should be read with the question "what changes between attempts?" — if the answer is nothing, it is not a retry, it is a delay before the same failure.

2. THIS IS THE DESIGNED CASE, ARRIVING EARLY. LOOP-SPRINTS.md plans for six parallel agents on one branch. It took exactly TWO concurrent writers — one human, one reactor — to break it. The path-lease and sprint-barrier machinery is aimed at agents conflicting with each other; nothing is aimed at an operator committing while the loop runs, which is the most ordinary thing that can happen.

3. THE GENERATED FILE CONFLICTS EVERY TIME, and that is fine. loop/data/graph.json is derived from the ledger, so two writers regenerate it from different states and collide on content. It resolves by REGENERATING, never by merging: take either side, run gen-loop-data.mjs --write, continue. That is LOOP-SPRINTS.md's "redo, not resolve" rule meeting its first real conflict, and the rule held.

Recorded separately because it bit while writing this bead: beads.mjs takes its body on the command line, so a body containing backticks is executed by the shell before the CLI ever sees it. This finding's first draft ran "git pull --rebase && git push" as a side effect of being written down. No damage — the pull refused on unstaged changes — but a knowledge tool whose input is shell is a knowledge tool that can act. A --body-file flag would end the whole class.

beads.title: Used r=1.4 for all four newly-swept solids, matching dodecahedron's existing value
beads.body: The ticket allowed 'r=1.4 or whatever keeps the block's existing style'. Kept 1.4 uniformly across all five solids in this block rather than varying r per solid, since the block's purpose is isolating the aniso variable — varying r per solid would conflate two things being tested and wasn't justified by anything in the ticket or the file's existing conventions. Would reverse this only if a future finding shows some solid's constellation() misbehaves specifically at r=1.4 (e.g. a degenerate clearance), which nothing here suggests.

beads.title: Turn 5 completed a coverage matrix with zero marginal detection value — the planner reasoned about the test's shape, not the code's
beads.body:
Turn 5 delivered exactly what lp-687d8d asked: the aniso sweep [1.2, 2.2, 3.5, 8] extended from dodecahedron-only to all five solids, seven lines, test file only. Clean work against its brief.

Its marginal DETECTION value is approximately zero, and the reason is structural rather than a mistake by the turn.

Measured: hardcode the metric response to the default aniso (2.2), ignoring the caller's. With turn 5's block, 17 assertions fail. With those seven lines deleted, 8 still fail. The bug is caught either way; turn 5 changed how loudly, not whether.

The reason: constellation() does not branch on solid. It maps ONE expression over spec.normals, so the anisotropy code path is identical for a tetrahedron and an icosahedron. An aniso-dependent bug is therefore solid-independent, and one solid swept across the aniso axis already covers it — which is precisely what the dodecahedron sweep was doing. Conversely a solid-SPECIFIC bug (a wrong entry in the normals table) shows up at the default aniso, which the per-solid exactness block already covers. The two existing blocks span the space between them; the new block is their intersection.

THE LESSON, which is about the planner and not this turn: it proposed completing a COVERAGE MATRIX — four solids times four aniso values, an obvious rectangle with a hole in it — by reasoning about the shape of the TEST. Detection value comes from the shape of the CODE: where it branches, and on what. A matrix is only informative along axes the implementation actually distinguishes.

Not worthless, and it should not be reverted: it is insurance against a future change that DOES branch per solid, and a per-solid failure line is more legible than inferring the same from dodecahedron alone. But it is insurance, not detection, and a planner that cannot tell those apart will keep proposing rectangles.

What a planner brief should carry as a result: propose coverage where the implementation BRANCHES. If the code path is shared, one representative case per path is the whole of the coverage, and the rest is decoration.

beads.title: Is the anisotropic squash something a player should FEEL, or something the game should hide?
beads.body:
Every summon so far is exact under a metric with aniso 2.2, so a solid is visibly squashed along Y. I cannot decide from here whether that reads as a deliberate material property of the foam — a thing you learn to exploit — or as a rendering bug the player fights. No gate measures this and either reading is internally consistent, so guessing sets the direction for every mechanic built on top of it.

DO: Open foam, summon a dodecahedron and an icosahedron side by side, and walk around them for a minute at eye level.

WATCH FOR: Whether the squash reads as the world having a grain you could use, or as the shapes being wrong.

SO THAT: If it reads as grain, I propose mechanics that USE the anisotropy — a source that only aligns along Y, a defense that is cheaper across the grain. If it reads as wrong, I propose a compensation pass that renders solids round while keeping the seed geometry exact, and the anisotropy stays a hidden implementation detail.

beads.title: Planning run 2026-08-04T23:17:51Z
beads.body:
A plan seat was staffed because the ready queue was starved. Output: proposals, born proposed, awaiting human promotion.

[turn ? — done] Read the vision, the five already-ready beads, and the full bodies of lp-f25c2f/lp-39d6e7/lp-484b7f to make sure nothing here duplicates them. All three already own the big moves toward playability (atomic multi-insert, real-pocket legality, frame budget) but none of them can land yet without a real pocket, which plant/ does not have — only solids.mjs and the standalone summon inspector exist there. So instead of proposing more geometry (explicitly out of scope per the vision's 'perfecting anything in plant/ that no level uses yet', and per lp-dff7a6/turn-5's finding that another coverage matrix has zero marginal detection value), I proposed two small, independent, inspector-facing tickets: one that gives the existing page a real player-caused fail state using an already-tested primitive (selfCompatible) that nothing currently surfaces, and one that hardens the page's own health check against the exact failure mode this repo keeps rediscovering (green and serving nothing) — because a playable page that silently 404s one of its two script imports is worse than an honestly red one. Filed one ask: whether the new fail state reads as a build constraint or as a broken slider, since that is a taste question no gate can answer and it directly determines whether I keep proposing inspector-scoped playability tickets next turn or switch to holding off until a real pocket exists.

beads.title: Scoped this turn's proposals away from geometry and away from the five already-ready beads
beads.body: lp-f25c2f, lp-39d6e7 and lp-484b7f already cover the three big moves (atomic multi-insert, real-pocket legality, frame budget) and lp-b80b67/lp-e8d94e are human-only. Proposing anything in that territory would either duplicate open work or require a real pocket that doesn't exist in plant/ yet. So both proposals here are inspector-facing UI work using primitives solids.mjs already has and already tests (selfCompatible), not new geometry — in line with the vision's 'what does not matter right now' list.

beads.title: The buildability indicator deliberately stops at self-compatibility, not obstacles or the hull
beads.body: lp-39d6e7 is scoped to legality against a real pocket's existing seeds and the indestructible hull, which needs machinery plant/ does not have yet. selfCompatible(con, minSeedGap) only checks a constellation's OWN seeds against each other and is already implemented and unit-tested in solids.mjs — it has just never been surfaced anywhere. Proposal 1 only surfaces that existing, narrower predicate, so it is independent of lp-39d6e7 and can land in either order without conflict or rework.

beads.title: Does the new self-compatibility fail state read as a build constraint, or as a broken slider?
beads.body:
Proposal 1 above adds a real fail state to the summon inspector — drag the inradius slider down and a solid flips from buildable to not, using the same rule reformPocket enforces elsewhere. But it is surfaced on a raw parameter slider in what is still a library page, not inside anything resembling a level, and I cannot tell from here whether that reads as 'the world has a build constraint you're bumping into' or as 'I turned a dial and got an error message'. This is one layer up from the already-open lp-7c8e6f (whether the anisotropic squash itself should be felt or hidden) — this one is about whether the FAIL STATE built on top of it lands as a mechanic.

DO: Once proposal 1 ships to plant.minomobi.com, pick icosahedron and drag the inradius slider down until the new buildable line flips from green to red.

WATCH FOR: Whether you instinctively try to fix it (raise r back up) before reading why it failed, or read the reason first — that's the difference between it landing as a mechanic and landing as noise.

SO THAT: If it reads as a mechanic, I'll keep proposing small inspector-scoped playability tickets like this one while lp-f25c2f/lp-39d6e7 are still in flight. If it reads as noise, I'll stop proposing anything UI-facing in plant/ next turn and only propose class-d analysis work until a real pocket exists to build an actual level against.

beads.title: Surface self-compatibility as a live buildable/not-buildable verdict in the summon inspector
beads.body: render() in plant/view.js should also return `buildable: selfCompatible(con, 1.5)`, importing selfCompatible from ./solids.mjs (already implemented and unit-tested — see the 'clearance' section of plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs). plant/index.html's #verdict panel gets a second, distinct line: '✓ buildable' (--ok) or '✗ own seeds too close — cannot summon here' (--bad), separate from the existing exactness line — a solid can be geometrically exact and still illegal to place: cube's minimum self-seed-gap is exactly 2r (an already-recorded finding), so at aniso 2.2 anything under r=0.75 already fails, well inside the page's existing r slider range of 0.6-3. This gives the inspector a real, player-caused fail state — drag r down and the verdict flips — which is a small, honest step toward the vision's #1 priority ('something playable, sooner than something perfect') without touching pockets, obstacles or the hull (that is lp-39d6e7's scope, not this one). PATHS (R3): plant/view.js, plant/index.html, plant/test/view.selftest.mjs. Nothing else. GATE (R2): extend plant/test/view.selftest.mjs with known-answer pairs already established in plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs's clearance section — tetrahedron r=1.0 aniso=2.2 buildable; icosahedron r=0.35 aniso=2.2 not buildable; cube r=1.0 aniso=2.2 buildable; octahedron r=0.3 aniso=2.2 not buildable — so the UI verdict can never silently drift from reformPocket's real rule. Do NOT add a full r-by-solid sweep; that is the discouraged coverage-matrix shape the vision and the turn-5 finding both call out. Four known-answer pairs already exercise both outcomes on both an axis-aligned solid (cube) and an off-axis one (icosahedron). R6: three files touched, purely additive, trivially revertable.

beads.title: Harden plant's /health to catch a page that is up but silently broken
beads.body: plant/worker.js's /health only fetches /index.html and reports ok:true if that 200s — but index.html loads solids.mjs and view.js as ES modules at runtime, and if either 404s or is served with the wrong content-type (a real failure mode for a Workers Static Assets deploy), /health stays green while the page renders nothing. worker.js's own comment names exactly this failure ('a worker that is up and serving nothing is the failure this repo keeps rediscovering') but the check does not cover it. Fetch /solids.mjs and /view.js alongside /index.html, report ok only if all three succeed, and include which path failed in the response body so a human debugging a green-but-broken deploy doesn't have to guess. PATHS (R3): plant/worker.js, plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs (new). GATE (R2): a new selftest that imports the worker's default export and calls .fetch(new Request('http://x/health'), { ASSETS: { fetch: mockFn } }) with a mock env.ASSETS.fetch returning canned Response objects for the three paths (all-200, index-only-200, and a middle-path-404 case), asserting the JSON body's ok flag and its failed-path field are each correct — Request/URL/Response are Node 18+ globals so this needs no wrangler runtime. R5: this is the same principle as the repo-wide finding 'Green is not proof: a deploy binds the custom domain or it changed nothing' — applied one layer down, to the page's own liveness check rather than to the deploy log. R6: one file modified (a superset of the current behaviour), one new test file, both trivially revertable.

beads.title: The health probe failed for two minutes after the site was live — one missing space, masked by continue-on-error
beads.body:
plant.minomobi.com went live on its first deploy (run 30959458804) and the health probe reported failure for two minutes after it was already serving. The step was continue-on-error, so the run went green with a masked failure — the worst of both readings.

The cause is one missing space. The worker answers with JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2), which emits:

    "ok": true

and the probe grepped for the string "ok":true with no space. It never could have matched.

What makes this worth recording rather than just fixing is how it read in the log. Attempts 1-7 printed a curl error each (could not resolve host, then HTTP 500 while the certificate issued). Attempts 8-12 printed NO error at all — just "not yet". That silence is the signature: curl had exited 0 and only the grep failed, which means the service was healthy and the check was broken. A health probe that pipes into a matcher has two failure modes that look identical from the outside, and only one of them is the service.

Three things follow:

1. MATCH KEYS, NOT KEY-VALUE PAIRS, unless the formatting is pinned. loop-plant now uses grep -qE with optional whitespace. deploy-loop.yml greps for the key '"beads"' alone and was never exposed to this, by luck rather than design.

2. A CHECK THAT CAN FAIL WHILE THE SERVICE IS HEALTHY IS WORSE THAN NO CHECK, because it teaches you to skip reading it. This one had continue-on-error on top, so it would have gone on silently reporting a false failure indefinitely.

3. THE PROVISIONING SHAPE IS NOW ON RECORD for the next surface created from a routes[] declaration: no DNS at all for ~10s, then Cloudflare error 1104 (HTTP 500) for ~60s while the certificate issues, then correct. Only a first deploy sees it, and it is indistinguishable from a genuine binding failure while it is happening, which is exactly why the tolerance existed and exactly why it had to be removed once it had done its job.

beads.title: A planner labelled work class-A against a gate file that does not exist — the validator cannot see the filesystem, so promotion must
beads.body:
The planner's second run proposed lp-4d3aa1 — "Harden plant's /health to catch a page that is up but silently broken" — labelled class-a, gated on:

    node plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs

No such file exists. Nothing in the system objected.

class-A does not mean "has a gate". It means CERTIFIED AGAINST AN EXISTING ONE (LOOP-WBS §2.3), and that distinction is the entire reason the fleet is allowed to run class-A unattended: the acceptance test is already there, already passing, and was not written by the turn being graded. A requirement whose test has yet to exist is a request FOR a test — different work, different risk, and the agent that takes it writes both sides.

Why nothing caught it: loop-apply-outbox validates the gate with validateGate(), which checks the verb allowlist and refuses shell metacharacters. It is deliberately PURE so it can run in the outbox validator with no filesystem, so it cannot ask whether a path exists. And `beads promote` — which does have a filesystem and does have a human in front of it — was checking that a class-A bead names a gate, not that the gate is real.

Fixed at promotion, because that is where both a filesystem and a human are available. Conservative by design: only tokens ending in a source extension are treated as paths, so a grep pattern containing a slash is not mistaken for a missing file. A DoR rule that cries wolf gets --forced past every time, and then it is not a rule.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is worth more than this instance: a validator that must stay pure cannot check anything about the world, so every constraint of the form "X must already exist" has to live at the boundary where the world is visible. The outbox validator can only ever check the SHAPE of a claim. Promotion is where the claim meets the repository. Anything asserting existence — a gate, a path, an artifact, a dependency outside the ledger — belongs in the second place, and putting it in the first feels safer while checking nothing.

The proposal itself is good and should be promoted once its test exists. The right decomposition is two beads: a class-d that writes plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs, then a class-a to harden /health against it. That is exactly the split the class system is for, and the planner produced the merged version because nothing in its brief told it that a gate it invents is not a gate it has.

beads.title: Demoted lp-6eb230: work promoted under the old vision must be re-judged under the new one
beads.body:
lp-6eb230 was promoted (by accident, during a test of the gate-existence guard) and is now demoted back to proposed. It is a good ticket and it is pointed the wrong way.

It adds a buildable/not-buildable verdict to the summon inspector: drag the radius down and the label flips red. Under the previous vision that was the right next step — a real fail state, cheaply. Under the vision as the operator has just restated it, it is "more inspector", which is now explicitly listed under what does not matter, and the bar for playable is "an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for". A slider turning a label red is not that.

Not dropped, because the underlying idea is sound and will matter once there is a pocket to place into: the same predicate that turns a label red is the one that refuses a summon. It goes back to the reviewer's desk to be judged against the new vision alongside everything else.

The general point, which is the reason this is a decision and not a silent edit: WORK PROMOTED UNDER AN OLD VISION MUST BE RE-JUDGED WHEN THE VISION CHANGES, and it will not re-judge itself. A queue is a set of bets placed under an understanding of what matters; change the understanding and the queue is stale, however well-formed each item still looks. Nothing in this system currently notices that — the reviewer sees the current vision and the current backlog, so it will catch this one by luck rather than by design. Worth building deliberately if the vision changes often.

beads.title: Used cube (not tetrahedron/icosahedron) for the centre-inclusion counter-example, via a closed-form r window rather than a hand-built synthetic seed set
beads.body: The ticket suggested a 'flattened constellation' as the natural shape. Cube turned out simplest and exact: because cube's normals are axis-aligned, its centre-to-(x or z)-neighbour gap is EXACTLY 2r with zero anisotropic contribution (dy=0), while its smallest neighbour-vs-neighbour gap is EXACTLY 2r*sqrt(2) -- both closed-form, no floating-point approximation risk (this restates the standing finding on cube's exact self-seed-gap). Since 2r grows slower in r than 2r*sqrt(2), there's a provable window (r in [1.5/(2*sqrt2), 0.75)) where centre violates and neighbours don't. Picked r=0.7 for comfortable margin on both sides of the threshold. Rejected building a hand-crafted seeds array outside constellation() -- using the real constellation() output keeps the test honest about what a real summon would produce, and keeps the reasoning auditable against the exact-2r finding already on record instead of introducing a new unverified geometric claim. Would reverse if a reviewer finds the arithmetic wrong when actually run -- but every step is closed-form (no sqrt of a difference near zero, no trig), so I'm confident in it without execution.

beads.title: The loop could only ever polish: class-A needs a gate that exists, so work needing a NEW gate was permanently unschedulable
beads.body:
The operator looked at plant.minomobi.com and said: "I notice this isn't the foam game with object placement, but an explainer for how it might be achieved." That is a description of the output. This is the mechanism, and it was structural rather than a matter of taste or prompting.

  1. Only class-A beads are dispatchable to the unattended fleet.
  2. class-A means CERTIFIED AGAINST AN EXISTING GATE.
  3. Therefore work needing a gate nobody has written yet can NEVER be dispatched.
  4. Therefore the loop can only ever refine things that are already tested.

The backlog proves it. Every roadmap item the vision now calls priority one was sitting there unschedulable the whole time:

  lp-b781be  Production feasibility oracle — the algebra      class=NONE gate=NONE
  lp-ce20ae  Object kinds: sources, processors, defenses, sinks class=NONE gate=NONE
  lp-39d6e7  Summon legality as a decidable predicate in a real pocket  class=b gate=NONE
  lp-f25c2f  Atomic multi-insert: reformPocket for a constellation      class=b gate=NONE

Meanwhile every turn the loop DID take — solids exports, an aniso sweep, a yaw case, an inspector — shared one property: solids.selftest.mjs already existed to grade them. The loop was not avoiding the game. It was structurally incapable of reaching it, and everything it could reach was a refinement of what it already had.

Worse, it looks like diligence from inside. Every turn passes its gate, the ledger fills with green, the curve would climb if it were measuring anything. A gate-graded loop drifts toward whatever is already gateable, and the drift is invisible precisely because the gates keep passing.

THE FIX: a bead may declare the gate it will CREATE (tag `creates-gate` plus the file in `gate`). It is dispatchable without a pre-existing gate, and it is judged HARDER than class-A, not softer:

  · the named file must NOT exist at promotion (promotion refuses it otherwise —
    a gate already present proves nothing about new capability);
  · it must EXIST after the turn;
  · it must PASS;
  · and the entire existing suite must still pass. New capability that breaks an
    old one is not new capability.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, and it must be said plainly: nothing here can tell whether the new gate ASSERTS anything. A test with no assertions passes exactly as green as a good one, and the agent writes both the code and the test that judges it — the self-certification hole from lp-20c414, now with the test file itself in scope. Promotion prints a warning for this reason. The review seat reading the diff and the judge's adversarial signal are the only real checks, and both are human-shaped judgements on a machine-shaped claim. A gate-creating turn is the one most worth reading.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part that transfers: A LOOP CAN ONLY BUILD WHAT IT CAN ALREADY MEASURE, UNLESS BUILDING NEW MEASUREMENTS IS ITSELF SCHEDULABLE WORK. Any system that gates its own work on pre-existing acceptance criteria will converge on the subset of the problem those criteria already cover, and will do it while reporting success. The escape is not a looser gate. It is making the construction of gates a first-class, gradeable act.

beads.title: A six-minute planning turn was discarded for a body 456 characters over a limit the brief never mentioned
beads.body:
A planning turn thought for six minutes, produced one proposal, and lost all of it to this:

    propose[0].body is 4456 chars, over the 4000 limit
    1 outbox file(s) rejected — the ledger was not modified for those

456 characters over. Rejection is deliberately all-or-nothing — a half-applied outbox is a corrupt ledger — so the whole turn went with it, and the loop then reported itself starved and asked for another planner. It would have kept doing that.

TWO SEPARATE MISTAKES, and only one of them is the number.

1. THE LIMIT WAS NEVER IN THE BRIEF. The planner was told at most 12 proposals and never told how long a body may be. It could not have complied except by luck. Any constraint the validator enforces and the prompt omits is a trap with a delay on it, and this class of bug will recur for every limit that lives only in the validator — check them against the brief.

2. THE CAP WAS TIGHT ENOUGH TO BITE GOOD WORK, which makes it worse than no cap. A well-written verifiable requirement is genuinely long: bounded paths, the acceptance test, the known-answer pairs that test should use, the findings that bear on it, what it deliberately leaves to a sibling. The best proposal this loop has produced ran past 3000 characters and every one was load-bearing. A cap that punishes that teaches the writer to be VAGUE, and a vague requirement is the one artefact this system cannot use — it is exactly the failure the whole DoR exists to prevent. Raised to 8000; flooding stays bounded by MAX_PROPOSALS x MAX_TEXT, which is under 100KB.

WHAT I GOT WRONG WHILE DIAGNOSING IT, worth recording because the reasoning was seductive: seeing the planner produce zero proposals, I assumed it had been squeezed between "make the game" and "only propose work with an existing gate" and had correctly concluded there was nothing legitimate to propose. That was a satisfying story, it fit the trap I had just found and written up, and it was wrong. The planner proposed something perfectly reasonable and a length check ate it. A tidy explanation that confirms the thing you just discovered deserves more suspicion than a messy one, not less.

beads.title: loop-apply-outbox.mjs's propose[] schema has no field for the creates-gate tag
beads.body: beads.mjs's cmdPromote requires a bead to carry the literal tag creates-gate (checked via tags.includes, not derived from class) before it's treated as gate-creating work (scripts/lib/beads.mjs createsGate()). But loop-apply-outbox.mjs's propose-entry handler only ever writes tags: ['proposed-by-agent', class-<cls>] — there is no propose[i].tags passthrough, so a planner cannot cause the resulting bead to carry creates-gate through the outbox JSON alone. Future planners: don't hunt for a tags field on propose[i]; say creates-gate explicitly in the body instead, as this turn does.

beads.title: Production feasibility oracle — gate 5, exact linear feasibility for acyclic recipe networks
beads.body:
Gate 5 (FACTORIO.md §2, §3) is the vision's top priority and the next unbuilt oracle: 'a factory is a flow network, so satisfiability is a feasibility question over a small non-negative linear system — exact, cheap, no search, no heuristics... the next real gate and the last one that is straightforwardly buildable.' PROMOTION NOTE: promote with both class-d and the creates-gate tag (beads promote lp-<id> --tag creates-gate) — the gate named below does not exist yet, and the outbox schema this proposal travels through has no field that can set that tag itself (this turn's 'loop-apply-outbox.mjs has no tags field' finding).

This formalizes the now-rejected placeholder lp-b781be into a concrete, one-turn, independently-dispatchable requirement, dropping lp-b781be's dependency on lp-ce20ae (also rejected, itself un-gated) by defining node kinds directly rather than waiting on a separate object-kinds bead.

Build plant/production.mjs — pure, dependency-free, node-and-browser, no unseeded randomness (the house rule solids.mjs states in its own header). Model a production network as three node kinds plus edges:
source: {kind:'source', id, resource, rate} — emits `resource` at up to `rate`/s.
processor: {kind:'processor', id, inputs:[{resource,rate}], outputs:[{resource,rate}], capacity} — at scale s in [0,capacity] consumes s*rate of each input, emits s*rate of each output.
sink: {kind:'sink', id, resource, demand} — needs >= `demand`/s of `resource`.
edges: [{from, to}] — id pairs; the resource is whichever one `from` emits that `to` accepts (throw if ambiguous or absent).

SCOPE, up front so the turn doesn't over-reach: v1 disallows FAN-OUT — every node has at most one outgoing edge — which is what keeps this 'small and exact' instead of a general LP needing a real solver. CONVERGENCE stays allowed, and is what makes multi-input recipes real: several producers (e.g. two sources) may feed one consumer's different (or same) input resources. Cycles are refused (topological sort must succeed) — recycling loops need a fixed-point technique this gate doesn't need yet. Record the fan-out restriction in the module's header comment, matching solids.mjs's style of naming the trap up front — a scoping call, not a taste question, so don't file it as an ask.

Core function: feasible(network) -> {ok, achieved:{sinkId:rate}, deficits:[{sinkId,resource,demand,achieved}], margin}. Topologically sort, then walk in order computing what each node ACTUALLY produces (not what it's rated for): a source produces its full rate; a processor sums incoming supply per input resource from converging edges, sets scale = min(capacity, min over inputs of supply/inputRate), emits scale*outputRate per output; a sink's achieved rate is the sum of its incoming supply. ok is true iff every sink's achieved >= demand. margin = min over sinks of (achieved-demand)/demand — this doubles as FACTORIO.md §3's difficulty dial ('the margin by which a recipe set is satisfiable is a difficulty measure, the same way parMin/parTarget band the walk today'); don't build that separately, it falls out of the same pass.

Refusals (thrown, one cause each, matching solids.mjs's throws() style): unknown node kind; duplicate id; edge naming an unknown from/to; a node with >1 outgoing edge (fan-out); a cycle; an edge whose resource can't be matched unambiguously; non-positive rate/demand/capacity; a processor with zero inputs or zero outputs.

Gate (new): plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, matching plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs's density and house style (named ok() assertions, a print label, real CONTROL cases proving the checker can FAIL) — per the standing findings 'class-A's gate certifies no regression, not the new behaviour — the agent writes the assertions it is graded by' and solids.mjs's own 'a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker.' Minimum coverage: a feasible chain with positive margin; CONTROL — same chain, source.rate lowered until infeasible, deficit names the right sink/resource; a two-input processor (A+B->C) fed by two converging sources, feasible only when both clear demand, with a CONTROL starving one input; capacity actually caps scale; a fan-out attempt throws; a cycle throws; determinism (two calls, byte-identical result); margin's sign/magnitude checked against a hand-computed value on a known-ratio example.

Also add one line for production.mjs to plant/CLAUDE.md's file listing, matching solids.mjs's entry — self-documentation, not a separate deliverable.

Bounded paths (R3): plant/production.mjs (new), plant/test/production.selftest.mjs (new, creates-gate), plant/CLAUDE.md (one doc line). All under plant/. Independent (R4): no deps; defines its own node types rather than waiting on any other bead. Carries memory (R5): cites the class-A-no-regression and checker-fails-correct-work findings above, and lp-b781be/lp-ce20ae as prior art. Reversible (R6): both code files are new — deleting them and the one doc line fully reverts the tree.

[turn 7 — done] Built plant/production.mjs — pure, dependency-free, node-and-browser — implementing gate 5: exact feasibility for an acyclic, at-most-one-outgoing-edge production network of source/processor/sink nodes. Core export feasible(network) topologically sorts (Kahn's algorithm, refuses on any cycle), walks in order computing ACTUAL throughput (source at full rate; processor scale = min(capacity, min over inputs of converged supply/inputRate), clamped to >=0; sink achieved = summed converging supply), and returns {ok, achieved, deficits, margin} where margin doubles as the FACTORIO.md §3 difficulty dial from the same pass. Every refusal the ticket named throws with one distinct cause: unknown kind, duplicate id, unknown edge endpoint, fan-out (>1 outgoing edge), a cycle, an edge whose emits/accepts intersection isn't exactly one resource, non-positive rate/demand/capacity, and a processor with zero inputs or zero outputs. Wrote plant/test/production.selftest.mjs in solids.selftest.mjs's house style: named ok() assertions with a print label, and every positive case paired with a CONTROL that must fail (starved chain, starved single input in a converging two-input recipe, capacity binding under ample supply, fan-out/cycle throwing with a paired non-throwing control that removes only the offending edge, absent vs ambiguous resource matching, one test per other refusal, and a determinism check comparing two calls byte-for-byte). Added one doc line for production.mjs to plant/CLAUDE.md. I do not have Bash in this turn's tool grant, so `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs` was not executed in-turn — the arithmetic in every assertion was hand-traced against the module's own algorithm (documented in the decisions below) rather than run, matching the precedent from lp-dfad42/lp-138b76's same structural gap. Confidence is high but this is inference, not execution.

beads.title: This turn's own gate is unverifiable in-turn — same structural gap as lp-dfad42 and lp-138b76
beads.body: The tool grant for this turn was Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash, so `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs` (this ticket's own GATE) could not be run before reporting done. Every assertion's expected number was hand-computed against feasible()'s documented algorithm (topological walk, scale = min(capacity, min supply/inputRate), sink achieved = summed converging supply) and traced through by hand for each test network — e.g. chain: source rate 10 -> proc scale=min(1,10/5)=1 -> gear 5 -> margin (5-4)/4=0.25; capacity test: both input ratios are 2 but capacity 0.3 binds -> achieved 0.3, margin -0.7. This is the third bead in a row with this exact gap (class-a/creates-gate tickets whose acceptance test is a shell command, dispatched to a turn with no shell). Repeating the standing recommendation a third time because it has not been fixed: either grant Bash to turns whose gate is a command, or make explicit in the ticket that gate execution happens downstream (CI/judge) rather than in-turn.

beads.title: network shape is { nodes: [...], edges: [...] } with kind-tagged node objects in one array
beads.body: The ticket describes three node shapes (source/processor/sink, each carrying its own `kind` field) and an edges array, but never states the top-level container shape. Chose a single `nodes` array holding all three kinds distinguished by `.kind`, plus a sibling `edges` array — mirrors solids.mjs's flat-object style and lets id-uniqueness be checked in one pass. Rejected a `{sources,processors,sinks,edges}` split: it would make cross-kind duplicate-id checking and topological walk order two-step instead of one, for no expressive gain. Reversible by construction — nothing outside production.mjs and its selftest depends on this shape yet.

beads.title: edge resource ambiguity is judged at the node-pair level, not the specific-edge level
beads.body: "the resource is whichever one `from` emits that `to` accepts (throw if ambiguous or absent)" is implemented as: intersect emits(from) with accepts(to); the edge is illegal unless that intersection has size exactly 1. Consequence: if a `from` and `to` node share two or more resources, EVERY edge between them is refused, even if a caller intended two separate edges to each carry a different one of those shared resources — there is no per-edge resource tag to disambiguate with. This matches the ticket's literal wording (matching is a property of the two nodes, not of one edge among several), and keeps the validator's fan-out/cycle logic simple, but it means "two same-kind converging pipes between the same pair of nodes" is unsupported in v1. Would reverse if a real recipe design needs that shape — the fix is an explicit `resource` field on the edge object, used when present and only inferred when absent.

beads.title: a network with zero sinks is vacuously feasible with margin 0
beads.body: feasible() defaults margin to 0 and ok to true when the sinks loop never executes (no sink nodes at all), rather than leaving margin as +Infinity or NaN. Not exercised by any required test case since every real recipe has a sink, but an empty-sinks network is reachable (e.g. mid-construction) and Infinity/NaN would leak into any caller doing arithmetic on margin. Would reverse if a future caller wants to distinguish "no sinks" from "sinks with zero headroom" — currently both read as margin 0.

beads.title: plant/CLAUDE.md has no existing per-file listing to match — added one line to the nearest section instead
beads.body: The ticket says to add a line "matching solids.mjs's entry" in plant/CLAUDE.md's file listing, but plant/CLAUDE.md has no such entry for solids.mjs (or view.js's implementation file) to match — its "What is served" section describes index.html/view.js/test/view.selftest.mjs in prose, not a table, and never names solids.mjs at all despite it being the primitive everything else depends on. Added a two-sentence paragraph for production.mjs in the same prose style immediately after that section rather than inventing a table the rest of the file doesn't have. A future ticket that wants a real per-file listing (solids.mjs included) is a documentation gap worth its own bead, not something to retrofit here.

beads.title: Wire production.mjs into an actual level: a concrete recipe network certified feasible, with margin surfaced as the difficulty readout
beads.body: Gate 5 (this bead) proves a recipe network CAN be checked; nothing yet defines a REAL one. The vision's #3 priority is 'A LEVEL SOMEONE CAN LOSE' — one source, one sink, a constraint that bites. Class-a once written, gated on the now-existing plant/test/production.selftest.mjs plus a new assertion file for the specific level's numbers: author a small, named recipe (e.g. plant/levels/level1.mjs exporting one network literal) using plant/production.mjs's node/edge shape, call feasible() on it, and assert ok is true with a small positive margin (a margin near zero is 'barely satisfiable' and is the interesting case for a puzzle, per FACTORIO §3's difficulty-dial framing) plus at least one CONTROL variant (e.g. lower a source rate) that feasible() correctly reports as infeasible with the deficit naming the right sink. This is the first concrete link from the abstract oracle to something a player-facing level could use, and it is independently gate-able against feasible() as it stands today — no other bead blocks it.

beads.title: Decide and document whether production.mjs's edge model needs an explicit resource tag for same-pair multi-resource pipes
beads.body: This turn's decision log records that feasible()'s edge resource is resolved by intersecting emits(from)/accepts(to), which makes ANY two edges between the same node pair with 2+ shared resources ambiguous and therefore refused, even when a caller intends each edge to carry a distinct one of those shared resources. Before this becomes a real limitation felt by a level author (see the sibling proposal above), decide: (a) leave it — a processor needing two distinct pipes to the same downstream node is an edge case v1 can keep refusing, or (b) add an optional `resource` field to the edge object that feasible()/analyse() prefers when present and only infers via emits/accepts when absent. This is a class-d scoping question (the answer changes the module's public shape, so it should not be silently expanded inside an unrelated ticket) rather than a mechanical fix.

beads.title: Turn 7's self-written gate killed 6 of 6 mutants — and two false SURVIVEDs were my own mutations failing to apply
beads.body:
Turn 7 was the first GATE-CREATING turn: the agent wrote both plant/production.mjs (gate 5, the production feasibility oracle) and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, the test that judges it. Promotion warned that a gate asserting nothing passes as green as one that does, so the gate was mutation-tested rather than trusted.

Six mutations, all killed:

  feasible() always returns true                  KILLED
  Math.min -> Math.max (capacity stops capping)   KILLED
  every >= / <= made strict                       KILLED
  topological cycle check deleted                 KILLED
  sink demand zeroed                              KILLED
  fan-out refusal removed                         KILLED

The design is honest about its own scope, which is the part that inspires most confidence: v1 refuses fan-out outright rather than approximating it, and says why in the header — with fan-out allowed, "how much of a shared output goes where" becomes a general LP needing a real solver. Refusing a case is a legitimate answer for an oracle; silently approximating it is not, and this one refuses and says so.

THE METHOD FAILURE, which is the reason this is worth recording. Two of my first attempts reported SURVIVED and both were wrong — my own mutations were no-ops. One replaced the bare string 'cycle' when the source says 'production: network has a cycle'; the other matched a single-quoted throw when the source uses a template literal with backticks. Neither edit changed a byte, and a mutation that does not apply is indistinguishable from a test that fails to catch it. Both report SURVIVED.

That is a false negative in the direction that matters: it accuses good tests of being weak, and if acted on it produces busywork "strengthening" tests that were already fine — or worse, erodes trust in a suite that deserves it.

THE RULE: assert the mutation applied before believing the result. Diff the bytes, count the occurrences, fail loudly when the target is not found. An unapplied mutation must be an ERROR, never a data point. This applies to every mutation run in this repo, including the ones already recorded — lp-c46a0c's selfCompatible survivor was verified by a subsequent fix killing it, so it stands, but it was luck rather than method.

beads.title: level.mjs — the pure certificate that a set of placed objects is both legal and produces a satisfiable factory
beads.body:
Build plant/level.mjs — the pure module that answers 'is this level buildable and winnable' by composing what already exists, not rebuilding it: solids.mjs's selfCompatible and pairGap (own-seed and pairwise-gap checks, both already exported — do not reimplement) and production.mjs's feasible() (also already exported — do not reimplement). This is the bridge FACTORIO.md's oracle table implies but nothing today builds: gate 4 (solid fidelity, built) plus this ticket's session-placement check answer 'is every summoned object legal', gate 5 (production feasibility, built) answers 'does the resulting factory meet demand', and nothing calls both together against one ordered list of placements — which is exactly the gap vision.md names ('you cannot place a source next to a processor and watch something flow... there is no failure that isn't a slider going red').

Scope, precisely:

1. `placementReport(objects, minSeedGap = 1.5)` — `objects` is an ordered array of `{ id, con }` where `con` is whatever solids.mjs's `constellation()` returns (has `.seeds`, `.aniso`, `.extent`). Walk the list IN ORDER. Each object must be self-compatible (`selfCompatible(con, minSeedGap)`) or it is refused with reason `'self-collision'`. Otherwise it must clear `minSeedGap` (via `pairGap`) against every EARLIER object that was itself legal, or it is refused with reason `'collides with existing summon'` naming which earlier id it hit. Return one result per object in input order: `{ id, ok, reason, blockedBy? }`.

2. `levelVerdict(objects, edges, minSeedGap = 1.5)` — run `placementReport`, then build a production.mjs network from ONLY the legal objects: each legal object must also carry a `node` field shaped exactly like a production.mjs node (see production.mjs's own docstring for the three node shapes). Drop any edge that references an illegal object on either end — a refused summon was never placed, so it cannot supply or demand anything; do not silently keep it in the network, or a level could 'pass' on a factory it could never actually stand. Call `feasible({nodes, edges})` on the surviving subset. Return `{ ok: everyPlacementLegal && network.ok, placement, network }`.

What this does NOT do: check placement against a real foam pocket's existing seeds or hull — that needs foamworld.js, which is outside plant/'s bounded paths and is lp-39d6e7's job, correctly class-b. This ticket is scoped smaller on purpose: legality among objects placed together in THIS session, nothing more. Say so in the file's header comment.

Test shape — match the house style in production.selftest.mjs and solids.selftest.mjs exactly: every positive case needs a paired CONTROL that must fail, every number is checked against a hand computation, never truthiness alone.
- Reuse solids.selftest.mjs's own fixtures: two tetrahedra 20 apart (that file's own `pairGap >= 1.5` case) placed in order must both return `ok: true`; the same two tetrahedra with the second recentred 0.5 away (that file's own CONTROL) must return the second as `ok: false, reason: 'collides with existing summon', blockedBy: <first id>`.
- A self-incompatible constellation (reuse solids.selftest.mjs's r=0.35 icosahedron CONTROL) must refuse with `'self-collision'` even as the very first object in an empty session.
- End-to-end: three well-separated placements (source, processor, sink — reuse production.selftest.mjs's first fixture's exact rate/capacity/demand numbers) wired with edges must return `ok: true` with the SAME achieved/margin numbers that file already asserts by hand. CONTROL: recentre the sink on top of the processor (a collision) — verdict must be `ok: false`, and the network result must show the sink's demand unmet because it was DROPPED from the network, not silently fed — assert the achieved value is absent or zero, proving the drop actually happened rather than being assumed.
